title: Jeremiah 29:24–32
context: The LORD then tells Jeremiah what to say concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite. Shemaiah has sent letters in his own name to all the people at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests. In those letters he says the LORD has made Zephaniah priest in the place of Jehoiada, to put in the stocks and shackles every man who is crazy and makes himself a prophet, and he asks why Jeremiah of Anathoth has not been rebuked, because Jeremiah has sent word to Babylon that the captivity is long, and that they should build houses and plant gardens. Zephaniah the priest reads this letter in Jeremiah’s hearing. Then the LORD’s word comes: Jeremiah is to send to all the captives concerning Shemaiah, because he has prophesied and the LORD did not send him, and he has caused them to trust in a lie. The LORD will punish Shemaiah and his offspring; Shemaiah will not have a man to dwell among this people, and will not see the good the LORD will do to his people, because he has spoken rebellion against the LORD. Shemaiah’s title “the Nehelamite,” the priest Zephaniah, and the Jehoiada named in the letter should be hedged; this Jehoiada is not to be assumed, without care, to be the famous priest of an earlier century. The stocks and the insult “crazy” are Shemaiah’s words about Jeremiah, not the book’s verdict on him. The charge is the same shared ground as in chapter 28 and in 29:21–23: an unsent word that makes people trust in a lie, and rebellion spoken against the LORD. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference, without inventing a new contrast. The good that Shemaiah will not see is the good already promised to the captives, including the return after seventy years.

verses.text: Concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall speak, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall speak, saying,” A new name is introduced, and Jeremiah is told to speak concerning him. “Nehelamite” may mark a family or a place; the verse does not explain it, and the identification should be hedged. The LORD is giving this instruction, as the following verses make clear; the content of Shemaiah’s own letters will be quoted inside it.

Arminian readers take the opening as the start of a real case against a named man among the exiles, a word Jeremiah is to speak, not a rumor left in the dark.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same heading as the LORD’s charge to Jeremiah: speak concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite, a man about whom a full word will now be given.

Shared ground: Shemaiah is named, and a speech is commanded. Further history of this man beyond this unit is not supplied here.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘Because you have sent letters in your own name to all the people who are at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, and to all the priests, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies says, “Because you have sent letters in your own name to all the people who are at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, and to all the priests, saying,” Shemaiah has written in his own name, to the people in Jerusalem, to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests. This Maaseiah is not to be merged, without care, with the father of the Zedekiah of verse 21; the names may coincide or not, and should be hedged. The fault already named is letters in his own name, a reach from Babylon back to the temple leadership.

Arminian readers hear a public, written campaign, letters that actually arrived, which the LORD now answers, a use of Shemaiah’s own name that still tries to move priests in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “because” as the ground of the word: Shemaiah sent letters in his own name to the people and the priests in Jerusalem, including Zephaniah.

Shared ground: the letters are the occasion. Zephaniah’s further office and dates may be left as the next verse and verse 29 present them.

verses.text: “The LORD has made you priest in the place of Jehoiada the priest, that there may be officers in the LORD’s house, for every man who is crazy and makes himself a prophet, that you should put him in the stocks and in shackles.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shemaiah has written, “The LORD has made you priest in the place of Jehoiada the priest, that there may be officers in the LORD’s house, for every man who is crazy and makes himself a prophet, that you should put him in the stocks and in shackles.” Shemaiah treats Zephaniah as appointed in Jehoiada’s place, and he wants men he calls crazy self-made prophets put in the stocks. The Jehoiada named here should be hedged and not assumed to be the priest of a much earlier reign. “crazy” and “makes himself a prophet” are Shemaiah’s insult, aimed at men like Jeremiah, not the book’s description of Jeremiah’s call.

Arminian readers hear a move to silence the letter’s word by force, a charge of madness meant to justify stocks and shackles, which the hearers can recognize as an attack on Jeremiah’s message about the long captivity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted sentences as Shemaiah’s own program: Zephaniah is to act as priest with power to bind those Shemaiah calls crazy and self-made prophets.

Shared ground: the stocks are Shemaiah’s proposal, and the insult is his. The notes should not adopt his language as the truth about Jeremiah.

verses.text: Now therefore, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who makes himself a prophet to you,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who makes himself a prophet to you,” The letter turns to a complaint: Zephaniah has not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth. “makes himself a prophet” is still Shemaiah’s charge, the claim that Jeremiah’s standing is self-made. Anathoth recalls the book’s opening, and need not be explained again at length.

Arminian readers hear the pressure on the priest in Jerusalem: he is being asked why he has not silenced Jeremiah, as if the letter to the exiles were an offense that ought already to have been punished.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same question as Shemaiah’s rebuke of Zephaniah for inaction against Jeremiah of Anathoth, whom Shemaiah describes as making himself a prophet.

Shared ground: the target is Jeremiah, and the demand is a rebuke that has not yet come. The next verse will quote the content Shemaiah hates.

verses.text: because he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, The captivity is long. Build houses, and dwell in them. Plant gardens, and eat their fruit?” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The complaint is “because he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, The captivity is long. Build houses, and dwell in them. Plant gardens, and eat their fruit?” Shemaiah reports, or nearly reports, the letter’s own counsel, and treats the long captivity as the offense. The wording here is close to 29:5 but not identical, and the two lines should not be forced into one exact form.

Arminian readers hear the real point of the quarrel: Shemaiah rejects the word that the captivity is long, and that the exiles should settle, dwell, and plant, the very life the LORD has commanded in this letter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same cited words as the reason Shemaiah wants Jeremiah rebuked: a message to Babylon that the captivity is long, with houses, dwelling, gardens, and fruit.

Shared ground: the contested message is the long exile and the call to settle. That is the letter’s own word, now opposed from among the captives.

verses.text: Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet.” Zephaniah does not, in this verse, put Jeremiah in the stocks. Zephaniah reads Shemaiah’s letter so that Jeremiah hears it. Motives the text does not state should not be invented; the act recorded is a reading in Jeremiah’s hearing.

Arminian readers take the reading as a real turning of the letter over to Jeremiah, which then becomes the occasion for the LORD’s word, rather than as a silent compliance with Shemaiah’s demand for shackles.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same report: Zephaniah the priest reads the letter in Jeremiah’s hearing, and the next verse will say that the LORD’s word then comes.

Shared ground: Jeremiah hears Shemaiah’s letter because the priest reads it. The book does not here describe a punishment carried out.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,” The answer to Shemaiah is not Jeremiah’s private irritation. The LORD’s word comes, as it came after Hananiah broke the bar, and Jeremiah will be told what to send.

Arminian readers take the heading as a fresh sending: the prophet answers a letter with a word he is given, not with a retort of his own invention.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the LORD’s word coming to Jeremiah after the reading, the initiative again God’s, and the content following in the next verses.

Shared ground: what follows is the LORD’s word. The verse is a simple opening, like other such headings in the book.

verses.text: “Send to all of the captives, saying, ‘The LORD says concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite: “Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you, and I didn’t send him, and he has caused you to trust in a lie,”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah is to send to all the captives, saying that the LORD says concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite, “Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you, and I didn’t send him, and he has caused you to trust in a lie,” The answer is to go to all the captives. Shemaiah has prophesied, the LORD did not send him, and he has caused them to trust in a lie. The three clauses match the charge against Hananiah in 28:15, and they are shared ground. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference, without inventing a new contrast.

Arminian readers hear a public correction meant for the whole captive community, so that the lie will not keep their trust, a word they can still receive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same message as the LORD’s verdict to all the captives: Shemaiah prophesied, was not sent, and caused them to trust in a lie.

Shared ground: the issue is an unsent prophecy that produced false trust. The traditions need not divide over that charge.

verses.text: therefore the LORD says, “Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his offspring. He will not have a man to dwell among this people. He won’t see the good that I will do to my people,” says the LORD, “because he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his offspring. Shemaiah will not have a man to dwell among this people, and will not see the good that the LORD will do to his people, “because he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.” The reason matches the word against Hananiah. The good not seen is the good already promised to the captives, including the return after seventy years. The note should stay sober and not enlarge the penalty beyond the verse.

Arminian readers take the exclusion and the missed good as a real, announced outcome of rebellious speech, a warning to the captives about whose word they trust, without turning the offspring into a subject for harsh speculation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same verdict: the LORD will punish Shemaiah and his offspring; no man of his will dwell among the people, and Shemaiah will not see the good the LORD will do to his people, because of rebellion spoken against the LORD.

Shared ground: the chapter ends with this judgment and this reason. The good promised to the people still stands; Shemaiah will not see it.
